_readme: The SHAPE of the brain's Cloudflare configuration. This file is tracked and
therefore holds placeholders only. Copy it to a private location outside
this repository — /etc/brain/cloudflare.json, root-owned, mode 0600 — fill
in the real values there, and point provision.py at that copy. Keys
beginning with an underscore are documentation and are stripped before
validation, because JSON has no comments.
python3 deploy/cloudflare/provision.py --state /etc/brain/cloudflare.json
python3 deploy/cloudflare/provision.py --state /etc/brain/cloudflare.json --apply
Nothing here is a secret and nothing here may become one: the API token
comes from CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN in the environment, the tunnel connector
token lives in the file named by tunnel.token_file, and a service token's
client secret is created by a human and never passes through this file or
through provision.py. The script refuses to start if it finds anything
shaped like a credential in here.
Two hostnames means two applications, deliberately. There are no OAuth
scopes on this tenant [verified 2026-08-23] — the authorization-server
metadata advertises none and the token response returns an empty scope — so
read versus capture cannot be a scope and has to be two audiences. The two
hostnames must NOT be merged into one multi-domain application: an OAuth
token issued through any domain of an application is valid for all of them,
which would make a read-only token work against the capture endpoint.
The audience of each application is assigned by Cloudflare, not declared
here. provision.py prints it under 'PRIVATE'; copy it into the endpoints
list in /etc/brain/brain-http.json, which is where the origin learns which
aud belongs to which hostname.

_why_dedicated: The brain gets its own tunnel rather than joining the host's existing
connector. All replicas of one tunnel share ONE ingress list and traffic
is spread across them with no affinity [verified 2026-08-23], so reusing
the host tunnel would put the brain's routes in the same configuration as
unrelated dev servers — and the ingress PUT replaces that list whole. A
dedicated tunnel is also what makes the first step of incident
containment possible: stop this connector, and only the brain goes dark.
tunnel.name: brain
_local_config_note: The host path of the connector's config file — deploy/cloudflared/config.yml
in the compose project, which compose mounts read-only at
/etc/cloudflared/config.yml. Adjust it to wherever this repository is
checked out on the VPS, or drop the key entirely when running
provision.py from a machine that does not have the file; the check is
_ingress_note: With config_src 'local' the connector reads its ingress from the mounted
config file and the API holds nothing to reconcile; provision.py verifies
that the file and this list agree, and refuses if they diverge. The list
is still load-bearing here because it is what drives the DNS step. The
service host is the compose service name — no host port is published, so
'brain:8787' is reachable only from inside the project network.

applications.name: brain — read and capture
_session_note: They are two separate clocks and the shorter one wins: a refresh grant
that outlives the Access identity session forces an interactive
re-login the client cannot explain. provision.py refuses a mismatch.

_note: localhost and loopback are enabled because they are required, not
as a convenience: with no such application configured, the team
domain's registration endpoint rejects http://localhost:<port>/...
and http://127.0.0.1:... [verified 2026-08-23], which is what Claude
Code, mcp-remote and the MCP Inspector all use. The setting is a
union across every Managed-OAuth application on the account, so this
is an account-wide relaxation and is recorded as one.
allowed_uris holds the non-loopback redirect URIs proven necessary
by the client qualification matrix — add one only with an observed
failure behind it.

policies._note: Exactly one identity. Not a group, not a domain.
policies.name: brain owner

_note: Service Auth for headless clients. The token is named, never
any_valid_service_token — that rule reads as 'service tokens are
allowed here' and means 'every service token in this entire account
is allowed here', including ones minted years from now for something
unrelated. provision.py refuses it outright and resolves this name to
a token_id at run time, because ids are per-account and cannot be
written down in a tracked file.
service_auth_401_redirect above cannot be turned on until this
policy exists, so the first run against a fresh account reports it
as blocked and the run after the token is created enables it.
policies.name: brain capture service clients

_service_tokens_note: provision.py never creates these. Cloudflare shows a service token's client
secret exactly once, in the create response, and never again — so a script
forbidden to print or persist a secret can only mint a credential nobody
can use. A human creates the token where the secret is displayed to them
and puts it straight into secret_file. provision.py does the parts a human
is bad at: it checks the token exists, that it is bound to the right
profile's policy, and that it is not about to lapse.
profile must match the application whose Service Auth policy names the
token; provision.py fails the run if a read-only credential is bound to the
2160h is the design's 90-day expiry; expiry_warning_days is its 7-day alert.
_notifications_note: Cloudflare's half of the alerting, and the only half that survives the VPS
being gone -- every other alarm in this system runs ON the box it is
watching. Two policies, because the account offers little else that is
honest [verified 2026-08-23 against available_alerts].
Read the tunnel one for exactly what it says: Cloudflare's own docs are
blunt that tunnel status 'only reflects the connection between cloudflared
and the Cloudflare network... A tunnel can appear Healthy while users are
unable to connect to an application' [docs 2026-08-23]. It fires when the
connector dies and stays silent when the brain behind it does.
There is deliberately no application-health policy: the only HTTP-level
notifier here needs a standalone Health Check, a paid add-on this
deployment does not have, and an empty one would look like coverage while
alerting on nothing.
tunnel_id is NOT written here -- it is per-account, and provision.py fills
it in from the tunnel it just reconciled. The owner must be a recipient;
add others freely.
There is no new_status filter and that is a finding, not an omission: the
account's own available_alerts advertises one for tunnel_health_event and
the API rejects every documented status with 17108 [verified 2026-08-23].
The alert therefore fires on every transition, healthy included.

notifications.name: brain tunnel unhealthy
notifications.description: The brain's connector stopped talking to the Cloudflare edge.

notifications.name: brain access service token expiring
notifications.description: A headless credential lapses in 7 days.

_dns_note: One proxied CNAME per ingress hostname, pointing at
<tunnel_id>.cfargotunnel.com. Proxied is not a preference: an unproxied
record for a tunnel hostname resolves to nothing that can serve it, and it
would take the request out of Access, which is the whole authentication
boundary. provision.py reconciles DNS LAST, because DNS is the step that
completes the reachable path — Access takes about 85 seconds to begin
enforcing on a new application [verified 2026-08-23], and that window is
spent on a name that does not resolve yet.
Nothing here deletes: this zone carries other hostnames on a different
tunnel, and a record of another type on one of these names stops the run
for a human to look at rather than being replaced.

dns.comment: brain remote MCP — managed by deploy/cloudflare/provision.py
